extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and practitioners of natural and social science; philosophers of science; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: A late-19th-century textbook treatment of the aims, concepts, limits, and methods of science, covering criteria for valid scientific conceptions, laws, inference, mechanism, probability, and biological evolution and heredity. The material is intended to guide how science should be practised and how scientific statements should be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science as classification of facts and basis for judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification of facts and the formation of absolute judgments upon the basis of this classification — judgments independent of the idiosyncrasies of the individual mind — essentially sum up the aim and method of modern science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science's function is to classify facts, recognize their sequence and relative significance, and form judgments that are true for any individual observer. Training in natural science is recommended to acquire this habit of mind. Anti-pattern: allowing personal feeling or private interest to determine scientific judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-elimination of personal bias in scientific argument
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific man has above all things to strive at self-elimination in his judgments, to provide an argument which is as true for each individual mind as for his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing arguments and evidence framed so they do not depend on individual perspective; use of classification and publicly accessible data to achieve impartiality. Examples: repeated measurements, standardized procedures. Scoring note: degree of self-elimination can be judged by reproducibility and independence from individual testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science is description, not metaphysical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: That all science is description and not explanation; the science of the future will replace knowledge by belief in the perceptual sphere, and reserve the term knowledge for the conceptual sphere — the region of their own concepts and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific statements should aim to describe relations among phenomena using concepts, not to assert ultimate metaphysical causes. Anti-pattern: treating mechanistic or material models as ultimate realities rather than conceptual shorthand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons of legitimate inference
rubrics_metrics.description: There are canons that delimit legitimate scientific inference — statements about the limits and rules for deriving valid inferences from sense-impressions and data (see: 'The Canons of Legitimate Inference').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inference must respect limits of perception and evidential support; inferences should be judged by their derivability from observations and by whether alternative hypotheses have been considered. The book discusses limits to other-consciousness and the scientific validity of ejects as part of these canons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity of conceptions and inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: A conception or inference has scientific validity only insofar as it can be connected to sense-impressions and to legitimate procedures of inference; conceptions must be deducible from perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge conceptions by testability, derivability from observations, and their role in organizing data. Avoid unverifiable metaphysical constructs. Examples: evaluating whether a proposed entity (ether, atom, etc.) functions as a useful conceptual tool tied to observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural law as a human-relative formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural law is relative to man; man is the maker of natural law. The words 'natural law' have two senses and confusion between them must be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scientific laws as human summaries of observed regularities, not as metaphysical prescriptions beyond observational scope. Evaluate laws for universality only with reference to the domain of observations and conceptual definitions used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and progress in formulating scientific law
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific law's universality and improvement are matters of progress in formulation; laws should be judged by their scope, precision, and ability to summarize phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer formulations that increase explanatory power and predictive scope while remaining tested by observation. Anti-pattern: claiming absolute universality where domain-limited evidence exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occam's razor / parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: William of Occam's Razor (parsimony) — prefer the simplest adequate hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple hypotheses account for data, select the one that makes the fewest new assumptions. Use parsimony as a methodological criterion; avoid unnecessary multiplication of entities. Note: 'simplest' must still be adequate to account for the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability vs provability — use of probabilistic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between the probable and the provable; probability theory is the proper tool to handle uncertainty and to reason about breaches in routine perception (Laplace's theory and its bases are discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use probabilistic models where certainty is unattainable; evaluate hypotheses by likelihoods rather than absolute proof. Guidance includes recognizing the bases of Laplace's theory and the limitations imposed by ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism as conceptual shorthand and limits to mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanism is not at the bottom of phenomena, but is only the conceptual shorthand by aid of which we briefly describe and resume phenomena; there are limits to mechanism ('The Limits to Mechanism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mechanical models as useful descriptions; do not conflate them with metaphysical truth. Evaluate applicability of mechanistic explanations case-by-case; beware of overextending mechanical analogies into domains where they fail (e.g., life, mind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity belongs to conceptual, not perceptual, world
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity belongs to the world of conceptions, not to that of perceptions — routine and necessity are conceptual products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing causal or lawlike claims, recognize that 'necessity' is assigned in conceptual schemata; empirical routines justify expectation but do not reveal metaphysical necessity. Anti-pattern: asserting absolute necessity from limited perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: classification, sequencing, and significance of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method comprises classification of facts, recognition of their sequence and relative significance, and forming judgments independent of individual mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scientific work on clarity of classification, explicitness of sequence/causal claims, and justification of claimed significance. Examples: robust taxonomies, temporal ordering of observations, explicit effect sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for defining and assessing 'cause' and 'effect'
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause and effect should be treated as routine of experience; first causes have no existence for science; force as cause and will as cause are analyzed and limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess causal claims by their operationalization in routines of experience, reproducibility, and the ability to embed them in predictive frameworks. Avoid invoking metaphysical 'first causes' as scientific explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of other-consciousness and treatment of ejects
rubrics_metrics.description: Other-consciousness as an 'eject' has limits to scientific validity; the limits to other-consciousness and the possibility of physical verification are recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in attributing mental states to others beyond what is inferable from observable evidence; require testable links when claiming scientific knowledge about minds and consciousness. Anti-pattern: asserting detailed inner mental states without behavioral or physiological correlates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mathematical and geometric constructs in describing motion and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts like point-motion, hodograph, curvature, slope (speed as slope) and the geometry of motion are conceptual tools for precise description of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise mathematical representations when they clarify relations and permit quantitative predictions. Evaluate correctness by internal consistency and empirical applicability. Examples: using velocity diagrams, time-charts, curvature-acceleration relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific conception of mass, force, and definitions of laws of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific conception of mass and force must be defined operationally (e.g., mass as ratio of units in accelerations); Newtonian laws are open to criticism and redefinition within conceptual schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mechanical postulates by their operational definitions and empirical tests (e.g., equality of masses by weighing). Be open to revising foundational definitions when better conceptual frameworks or data arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for biological concepts: life, mechanism, heredity, and selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Biology requires precise conceptual definitions (e.g., living vs lifeless, mechanism and life, definitions of selection and the factors of evolution). Natural selection, variation, and heredity are framed as scientific concepts to be tested and measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate biological hypotheses by clarity of definitions, empirical measures (variation types, correlation, heritability), and integration with experimental and observational evidence. Anti-patterns: vague 'vital forces' or metaphysical life-principles as scientific substitutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative criteria for heredity and inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Heredity should be measured quantitatively (coefficients of heredity, regression, correlation); concepts include blended vs particulate inheritance, exclusive inheritance, reversion, prepotency, bi-parental inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statistical methods (frequency curves, correlation coefficients, regression lines) to quantify inheritance. Use pedigree analysis, measures of mid-parent correlation, and tests for exclusive vs blended inheritance. Scoring: stronger evidence when multiple quantitative indices concur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors of evolution: variation, correlation, selection, and unsolved problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolutionary change is to be analysed in terms of factors: continuous and abnormal variation, correlation, types (individual and racial), and selection (natural, sexual, genetic), with an emphasis on defining and measuring these factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evolutionary explanations by how well they specify and measure variation, demonstrate selection mechanisms, and account for correlation among traits. Recognize outstanding unsolved problems and avoid overconfident causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statistics and theory of errors in science
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical theory (frequency curves, regression, correlation, theory of errors) is part of the theory of observation and measurement in science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess data quality and inferential claims by applying error theory, appropriate summarizing statistics, and tests of significance. Use tables and graphical displays to reveal distributional properties and departures from model assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between abstract (precise) and synoptic (descriptive) sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish precise (abstract/mathematical) sciences from synoptic/descriptive sciences and recognize their different aims and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating scientific work, identify whether the contribution is conceptual/mathematical abstraction or descriptive/synoptic classification, and judge it by the appropriate standards: formal rigor for abstract work, comprehensiveness and clarity for synoptic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of imagination and aesthetic judgment within scientific method
rubrics_metrics.description: Science and the imagination cooperate: imagination must be disciplined for scientific use; science also interfaces with aesthetic judgments though different standards apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value imaginative hypothesis-generation but require empirical testing and logical discipline. Avoid treating aesthetic appeal as evidence of scientific truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological humility: limits of scientific method and the danger of metaphysics
rubrics_metrics.description: The author repeatedly emphasizes the limits of scientific method and warns against metaphysical intrusion; science must not cloak the unknown with undefinable phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims against what can be shown by observation and inference; flag when terms are being used to conceal ignorance. Encourage precise language and explicitness about limits of evidence.
